question: Since late 2021, the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has been under assault by the M23 Movement, reportedly supported by Rwanda and its army, according to several United Nations reports.

In a 2022 report, the non-governmental organisation Global Witness1 noted that Congolese minerals, including those contributing to the conflicts, continue to be smuggled into Rwanda and exported as Rwandan minerals. On 19 February 2024, the Commission and the Rwandan Government signed a memorandum of understanding2 on critical raw materials.
Discussions are also under way regarding a security and military cooperation pact3. 1.

In a context of escalating violence in the east of the DRC, does the Commission plan to propose further sanctions against individuals responsible for violating human rights and sustaining armed conflict, instability and insecurity in the DRC?

To use the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument, at least 93 % of funding has to meet the requirements of the Development Assistance Committee of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Will this instrument be used for critical raw material projects in Rwanda and, if so, what measures is the Commission taking to avoid promoting the illegal smuggling of critical raw materials and the intensification of regional conflicts?
Is the Commission considering extending the list of conflict-affected and high-risk areas to neighbouring and transit countries such as Rwanda?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2024) The autonomous sanctions regime regarding the Democratic Republic of the Congo is subject to a rigorous review every year. This is a ‘dynamic’ exercise: the EU can expand/reduce the list or consider other restrictive measures depending on how the situation evolves. Any decision on further sanctions is for the Council to take with unanimity.

The Memorandum of Understanding signed with Rwanda1 intends to support the sustainable and responsible sourcing, production, and processing of raw materials. The goal is to increase traceability and transparency, to fight illegal trafficking of minerals and to support Rwanda’s engagement with the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative to increase due diligence and traceability.

Such activities fit within the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation - Global Europe Instrument and with the criteria set by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development to official development assistance, namely because of their primary objective to benefit the recipient country’s population and overall economic development.

The list of conflict-affected and high-risk areas2 is not exhaustive. It does not substitute nor replace the broader due diligence efforts required by the EU importers of minerals and metals falling under Regulation (EU) 2017/8213. Importers sourcing from areas, which are not mentioned on the list, remain responsible to comply with the due diligence obligations under the regulation.
